I

The Grinder

Fiorenzato E64 Evo Pro

The E64 Evo Pro is a 64 mm flat-burr commercial grinder built for on-demand dosing — it grinds fresh for each shot rather than sitting pre-ground in a hopper, dosed through a programmable touchscreen rather than a mechanical doser.

Grind size is set with a stepless micrometric adjustment collar, so there are no click-stops to count. Dial in gradually and taste — or better, time the shot — rather than chasing a specific number on the collar. There is no single correct setting: only what lands the shot in the 25–30 second extraction window (see Coffee Bar Manual, Espresso Basics). Adjust in small increments and re-taste.

Specifications

Burr Size64 mm
Burr TypeFlat
DosingOn-demand
AdjustmentStepless (no click-stops)

II

The Espresso Machine

Sanremo Zoe Compact, 2 Group

The Zoe Compact is a 2-group machine with independently PID-controlled boilers per group — each side can be dialed to its own brew temperature, useful for running more than one bean on the bar at once.

Temperature stability depends on a full warm-up before service. A machine that is merely powered on is not necessarily ready — give the boilers and group heads time to stabilize before pulling shots for guests.

Specifications

Groups2
Boiler ControlIndependent PID per group
Warm-Up Time30–45 min before service

III

Steaming Milk

Milk Texturing

Milk texturing is achieved by combining air and steam near the surface of the milk as it expands, until the desired texture is reached. Different drinks call for different textures — dry for a cappuccino, wetter for a latte — so proper technique is essential to get good, consistent results every time.

Before You Start

Drink Size. This relates to the pitcher size and how much milk you'll be using — use the right pitcher and portion your milk to the drink, to help reduce waste.

Milk Temp. The ideal range for dairy is 145°F–155°F. Standard dairy alternatives can usually tolerate a maximum of about 145°F before breaking down in texture; "Barista" style alternatives can typically withstand higher temperatures and texture well.

Milk Texture. Texturing is a race against temperature — know before you start whether the drink calls for a dry, velvety texture (like a cappuccino) or a wet, silky one (like a latte).

Setup & Target

Target Temperature (Dairy)145°F – 155°F
Dairy Alternative — Max Temp~145°F (higher for "Barista" style alternatives)
Pitcher Fill (before steaming)1/3 – 1/2 full
Starting Position — Tip DepthJust below the surface, pitcher angled left or right — never centered

Technique

  1. Choose the right size steaming pitcher for the drink.
  2. Portion the milk to the drink's size and texture; use a measuring device if needed.
  3. Purge the steam wand into the drain tray for a couple of seconds to clear any condensation.
  4. Get into the Starting Position: wand tip just below the milk's surface, pitcher angled left or right (never centered) so the milk can whirlpool.
  5. Steam with enough pressure to create a gentle vortex — too little pressure causes a high-pitched squeal or rumble.
  6. As the milk starts to whirlpool and expand, slowly draw the pitcher down along the wand, keeping the tip just submerged near the surface.
  7. Once the texture is right, submerge the wand fully and continue heating to the target temperature.
  8. Turn off the steam wand.
  9. Set the pitcher aside.
  10. Purge the wand and wipe it clean with the wand towel.
  11. Groom the milk. this step is often skipped, but it finishes the texture, not just the look. Tap the pitcher on the counter, then swirl until the milk has a glossy sheen, like melted ice cream or wet paint.
  12. Pour into the center of the drink or crema.
  13. Clean the pitcher immediately — never put a dirty pitcher back in the fridge.
Never re-steam milk that has already been steamed — for quality control and to avoid health hazards.
IV

Barista Tools

The Kit on the Bar

Tools

Tamper (58 mm, flat base)
  • Distribute the grounds evenly before tamping.
  • Tamp level and firm, straight down — consistent pressure, not forced.

An off-level tamp is one of the most common causes of channeling.

WDT Tool (Fine-gauge tines)
  • Stir through the dose in a circular motion after grinding, before tamping.
  • Break up any clumps and redistribute the grounds evenly across the basket.

Especially useful on darker roasts, which clump more from surface oils.

Digital Scale (0.1 g precision)
  • Weigh the dose before grinding.
  • Weigh the shot as it pulls, to hit the target yield.

Dose, yield and time together — not the clock alone — is what makes a shot repeatable.

Milk Pitchers (12 oz / 20 oz / 32 oz)
  • Match the pitcher to the drink — a smaller pour is easier to control in a smaller pitcher.
  • Fill no more than halfway before steaming, to leave room for the milk to expand.

Rinse immediately after each use — dried milk is the hardest to get out.

Knock Box (Rubber-lined)
  • Knock the spent puck out of the portafilter with a firm, single motion.
  • Empty and rinse it out through service, not just at close.

A full knock box slows everyone down — empty it before it's overflowing.

Puck Screen (58 mm)
  • Place on top of the dose before tamping.
  • Wipe clean between shots; it keeps the group head cleaner and reduces channeling.

Not a substitute for a good distribution and tamp — it just keeps the mess contained.

Cleaning Kit (Blind basket, group brush, detergent)
  • Backflush at the intervals set out in The Espresso Machine's Startup & Care.
  • Brush the group head daily; deep-clean the shower screen and gasket weekly.

A clean group head is a taste issue before it's a hygiene one — old coffee oils turn rancid fast.

Workstation Setup

Lay the station out in the order of the shot — grinder, portafilter, tamper, machine — left to right (or mirrored, for a left-handed bar), so every shot moves in one direction without doubling back.

Keep the knock box within arm's reach of the grinder, not the machine — pucks get knocked out right after grinding a new dose, not after pulling a shot.

Separate cloths by task: one dry for wiping the steam wand, one damp for the group heads and drip tray, and never the two swapped — milk residue on a group-head cloth spreads dried milk instead of removing it.
